card: Paper card. Question: What are the physical origins of the exceptional high-temperature strength and strength retention in refractory body-centered-cubic (BCC) high-entropy alloys (HEAs)?. System: NbTaTiV (nominal Nb25Ta25Ti25V25 at.%) and CrMoNbV (nominal CrMoNbV at.%); search space includes the 10-component Al-Cr-Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-V-W-Zr family.. Processing: Arc-melting of 99.9 wt.% purity elements under argon atmosphere followed by drop-casting into cylindrical rods; NbTaTiV homogenized at 1473 K for 3 days then water-cooled; CrMoNbV tested in the as-cast state.. Test conditions: Uniaxial compression at strain rates of 1 × 10−3 s−1 (NbTaTiV) and 2 × 10−4 s−1 (CrMoNbV); temperatures up to 1173 K; in situ neutron diffraction and high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) performed during deformation.. Findings: Neutron diffraction peak broadening analysis yielded q values of -0.6 to -0.4 for NbTaTiV and -2 for CrMoNbV, consistent with edge dislocations and distinct from screw dislocations (+1.9 to +2.1).; Bright-field STEM stereographic analysis of NbTaTiV deformed at 293 K showed 75% (58 of 77) of dislocations were of edge character.; Bright-field STEM stereographic analysis of CrMoNbV deformed at 293 K showed 56% (23 of 41) of dislocations were of edge character.; At 1173 K, edge dislocations remained dominant with 82% (27 of 33) in NbTaTiV and 64% (81 of 127) in CrMoNbV.; The CrMoNbV alloy exhibited the highest reported strength at a homologous temperature of 1173 K.; A computationally guided search over 10^7 BCC HEA compositions identified over 10^6 possible ultra-strong high-temperature alloy compositions.; Theoretical predictions for NbTaTiV strength were lower than experimental values by ~300-500 MPa, attributed to 1.6 at.% O+N interstitial impurities.. Mechanism: In complex HEAs, fluctuations in local solute arrangements create large local variations in potential energy, forcing edge dislocations to adopt a low-energy wavy structure; plastic flow requires thermal activation to overcome large energy barriers created by adjacent high-energy environments, enabling high strength retention at elevated temperatures.. Limitations: The theory does not capture the strength plateau observed at 973–1273 K in many BCC HEAs; neutron pattern quality for CrMoNbV was lower than for NbTaTiV, especially at low plastic strains; the theory assumes a homogeneous average alloy which may not fully capture local complexities.. Future work: Propose fabrication and testing of specific alloys (Mo5W2.5CrZrHf, Mo2.5W2.5CrZrHf, Mo6WCrZrHf, Mo2.5TaWV2.5CrZrHf) with predicted strengths of ~2.5-3 GPa at 1300 K; combine design strategy with detailed thermodynamics and high ductility criteria to discover multi-objective alloys.. Quote: "Here we show, using integrated in-situ neutron-diffraction (ND), high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM), and recent theory, that the high strength and strength retention of a NbTaTiV alloy and a high-strength/low-density CrMoNbV alloy are attributable to edge dislocations."

card: Paper card. Question: How do specific alloying elements (Nb, Ta, Ti vs. Cr, Mo) influence the deformation mechanisms and creep resistance of Ni-based superalloys at high temperatures?. System: Two single-crystal Ni-based superalloys: ME3 (9.1 wt% η phase formers: Nb, Ta, W, Hf, Ti) and ME501 (13 wt% η phase formers), with ME501 having higher Ta, Hf, and Nb and lower Co and Cr compared to ME3.. Processing: Single crystals were cast, heat-treated to form a bimodal γ-γ′ microstructure, and machined into compression cuboids (1:1:2.5 ratio) via Electrical Discharge Machining (EDM).. Test conditions: Monotonic compression creep tests at 760 °C on [001] oriented samples; ME3 tested at 414 MPa and ME501 at 552 MPa to achieve comparable strain rates of 5 × 10⁻⁹ s⁻¹.. Findings: ME501 exhibited remarkably improved creep resistance compared to ME3 at 760 °C and 552 MPa.; Nanotwinning contributed up to 50% of the plastic strain in ME3 but was not operative in ME501.; In ME501, shear-induced solid-state transformation from γ′ to η phase occurred along stacking faults, whereas ME3 showed segregation of γ-formers (Cr, Mo).; Atomic resolution EDX confirmed Ta and Nb segregate to Wyckoff 2a positions and Al and Ti to Wyckoff 2d positions of the η phase at faults in ME501.; The energy barrier for thickening stacking faults into nanotwins was 364 mJ m⁻² for pure Ni₃Al, 481 mJ m⁻² for ME501 (random solid solution), and 743 mJ m⁻² for the η-phase-segregated fault in ME501.; Energy release upon atomic reordering for twin formation was 375 mJ m⁻² for pure Ni₃Al but only 15 mJ m⁻² for ME3.; Isolated stacking faults in ME501 were identified as superlattice extrinsic stacking faults (SESFs) constrained to the γ′ phase.. Mechanism: The authors propose a 'phase-transformation strengthening' mechanism where high concentrations of η-phase formers (Nb, Ta, Ti) segregate to stacking faults, inducing a shear-induced transformation to a nanoscale η phase. This η phase creates a low-energy structure that significantly increases the energy barrier for the thickening of stacking faults into nanotwins, thereby suppressing the deleterious nanotwinning deformation mode. Conversely, in alloys with γ-formers (Cr, Mo), the fault transforms into a γ-like region that lowers the energy barrier for twin formation.. Limitations: The text notes that the ability to predict mechanical properties for a given alloy remains a major challenge and that the characterization of specific elements in compositionally complex superalloys has historically been qualitative and empirical.. Future work: The authors suggest that this mechanism may be further manipulated through alloying and processing to improve the high-temperature properties of next-generation superalloys for critical structural applications.. Quote: "specific alloying elements inhibit the deleterious deformation mode of nanotwinning at temperatures above 700 °C"

card: Paper card. Question: What are the unique elastic and plastic deformation mechanisms of a single-phase BCC NbTaTiV refractory high-entropy alloy at room temperature and elevated temperatures, and how do they compare to conventional BCC alloys?. System: Nb23.8Ta25.5Ti24.9V25.8 (nominally Nb25Ta25Ti25V25 atomic %). Processing: Arc melting under argon atmosphere from 99.99% purity elements, melted 10 times, drop-cast into 4-mm diameter rods, sealed in quartz tubes, homogenized at 1200°C for 3 days, followed by water cooling.. Test conditions: In situ neutron diffraction compression tests at RT, 500°C, 700°C, and 900°C with strain rate of 1 × 10−4 s−1; Resonant Ultrasound Spectroscopy (RUS) from 100 to 650 kHz; First-principles DFT calculations at absolute zero and RT; Machine Learning predictions; HAADF-STEM imaging of 15% deformed samples.. Findings: Yield strength decreased from 1064 MPa at RT to 595 MPa at 900°C.; Work-hardening exponent decreased from 0.2732 at RT to 0.1199 at 900°C.; The alloy exhibits elastically isotropic deformation behavior at RT (Zener anisotropy AZ ≈ 1.2, Universal anisotropy index AU = 0).; Elastic anisotropy gradually increases at elevated temperatures but shows much smaller variation (AZ from 1.2 at RT to 1.6 at 900°C) compared to conventional alloys.; The dominant mobile dislocations during plastic deformation are edge dislocations (<111> {110}), unlike conventional BCC metals where screw dislocations often dominate.; Single-crystal elastic constants calculated via DFT show good agreement with experimental neutron and RUS data, with relative errors of -15.9% (Young's), -16.6% (shear), and -6.0% (bulk) at RT.; The alloy maintains a single BCC solid solution phase with grain sizes of 200 to 400 μm up to 900°C.; Pugh ratio (K/G) and Poisson's ratio (ν > 0.26) indicate the material is intrinsically ductile.. Mechanism: The authors argue that the severely distorted lattice in the HEA, caused by the random distribution of multiple elements with different atomic radii, leads to compositional fluctuations that deviate edge dislocation cores from their neutral planes. This creates wavy dislocation lines, which substantially reduces the mobility of edge dislocations, making them the dominant mobile character compared to conventional BCC metals where edge dislocations annihilate easily.. Limitations: The text notes that the validity of theoretical calculation methods for designing elastically isotropic and ductile BCC HEAs was previously lacking experimental validation, though this paper addresses that. It also mentions that the ML model predictions are somewhat unexpected because the Materials Project database contains ordered compounds, not disordered alloys like HEAs, and lattice distortion effects might cause less accurate results.. Future work: The authors state these discoveries may facilitate the development of possible alloy systems for structural material applications and provide a road map toward the discovery and production of newly designed polycrystalline materials.. Quote: "The dominant type of mobile dislocations during plastic deformation could be edge dislocations, which is different from conventional BCC metals."

card: Paper card. Question: Can a quaternary equimolar high-entropy alloy (CoCrFeNi) composed of base metals exhibit higher electrochemical hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) activity in acidic solutions than its individual component metals or platinum?. System: CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy (equimolar composition: 26.5:23.7:25.0:24.8 Co:Cr:Fe:Ni), compared with pure Co, Cr, Fe, Ni foils, SS304, and Pt electrodes.. Processing: Arc-melting of 99.99+% pure Co, Cr, Fe, and Ni powders in an argon atmosphere on a water-cooled copper hearth with a tungsten electrode; the button was turned over and re-melted multiple times for homogeneity, sliced into wafers (ca. 8 × 5 × 1 mm3) by electrical discharge machining, and mechanically polished with 0.2 μm alumina powder.. Test conditions: Electrochemical testing in 0.5 M H2SO4 (pH 0.3) at ambient temperature and pressure; linear sweep voltammetry at 20 mV/s from 0 to −0.7 V; stability tested by cycling between 0 and −0.45 V at 20 mV/s for 1000 cycles (12.5 h); XPS performed in UHV (1 × 10–10 Torr) with O2 dosing up to 1000 L.. Findings: The CoCrFeNi HEA exhibits an overpotential of only 60 mV relative to Pt for the HER at a current density of 1 mA/cm2 in 0.5 M H2SO4.; The HEA is more active than each of the individual base metals (Co, Cr, Fe, Ni) by 250 mV or more at 1 mA/cm2.; Ni is the most resistant to oxidation among the components; no Ni oxide formation was detected even after 1000 L of O2 exposure in UHV.; Cr oxides form quickly (within 5 L O2) and saturate well below 500 L O2, while Fe and Co saturate around 500 L O2.; The HEA shows high stability with only ca. 0.1 wt % total weight loss after 1000 electrochemical cycles, with no preferential loss of any particular metal.; Theoretical modeling predicts that the HEA surface becomes partially oxidized in acidic solution, with 19 of 36 fcc sites oxidized and 18 open sites populated with H.; The differential binding strength of H on the partially oxidized HEA surface is within ca. 0.1 eV of the Pt(111) value for approximately 55–70% of the open sites.. Mechanism: The authors propose that upon exposure to ambient O2, the HEA surface becomes nearly fully oxidized except for Ni-rich sites; under cathodic bias in acidic solution, these sites are partially reduced to form a partially oxidized surface where adsorbed O atoms moderate the hydrogen adsorption energy (ΔGH*) to a level close to that of Pt, thereby enhancing HER activity compared to the un-oxidized base metals.. Limitations: The study notes that no finite-size surface model can uniquely represent the HEA surface and that the theoretical approach uses an approximate surface model; the UHV oxidation experiments do not directly probe surface oxidation in electrochemical settings.. Future work: The authors suggest that a small increase in the concentration of Ni could strengthen H adsorption slightly further, making the alloy even more active for HER, and call for a systematic approach to guide the substitution of precious metals with earth-abundant metals using theoretically predicted random alloy compositions.. Quote: "the HEA exhibits an overpotential of only 60 mV relative to Pt for the HER at a current density of 1 mA/cm2."

card: Paper card. Question: Is it feasible to produce the refractory metal high entropy alloy W20Mo20Ta20Nb20V20 via in-situ alloy formation using laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB/M) from elemental powders, and how do process parameters influence defect formation, microstructure, and phase composition?. System: W20Mo20Ta20Nb20V20 (refractory metal high entropy alloy) fabricated from a heterogeneous mixture of elemental W, Mo, Ta, Nb, and V powders.. Processing: Laser Powder Bed Fusion (PBF-LB/M) using an AconityMINI machine with a 1 kW fiber laser (1080 nm) on a Mo substrate in Argon atmosphere (<25 ppm O2). Two parameter sets were used: Set A (600 W, 800 mm/s, 120 µm hatch, 125 J/mm³) and Set B (100 W, 100 mm/s, 45 µm hatch, 889 J/mm³). Vanadium powder content was increased by a factor of 1.5 to compensate for evaporation.. Test conditions: Samples (6 × 6 × 6 mm³) were analyzed via optical microscopy, SEM, EBSD, TEM, and microhardness testing. Microhardness was measured as HV0.1. Cooling rates are estimated at 10⁶ K/s.. Findings: Relative densities reached 99.8% for parameter set A and 99.5% for parameter set B.; A single bcc-phase was confirmed by EBSD and TEM, consistent with vacuum arc melted samples.; Average grain size was 16.3 µm for PBF-LB/M B, which is more than four times smaller than the 80 µm reported for vacuum arc melted samples.; Parameter set B (higher volumetric energy density) resulted in fewer undissolved tungsten particles compared to set A.; Parameter set A exhibited smaller cracks than set B, which showed wider cracks due to higher internal stress.; Microhardness of the coarser structure (Set A) was 561 ± 17 HV0.1, while the finer cellular structure (Set B) was 614 ± 21 HV0.1.; Elemental segregation was observed: V concentrated in interdendritic areas, while W and Ta were predominantly in intradendritic areas.; Solidification mode shifted from dendritic (Set A) to cellular (Set B) based on growth rate (R) and temperature gradient (G) conditions.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the formation of undissolved W particles to the high melting point of tungsten, which requires high volumetric energy input and slow scan speeds to dissolve. Cracking is caused by internal stresses from the PBF-LB/M process combined with the alloy's low room temperature ductility and brittle grain boundaries (likely due to O and N impurities). The microstructure (dendritic vs. cellular) is controlled by the ratio of growth rate (R) to temperature gradient (G), where higher R and lower G favor dendrites, while lower R and higher G favor cellular structures.. Limitations: Samples contained cracks and undissolved tungsten particles; completely defect-free samples were not produced. The study notes that the alloy has limited room temperature ductility and fracture toughness.. Future work: The authors suggest using a high-temperature (>600 °C) build-platform heating device and/or high-purity powder with low O and N content to achieve crack-free processing. They also propose verifying if more recently developed refractory metal high entropy alloys with increased room temperature ductility can be processed without high-temperature heating.. Quote: "The relative density of the samples with a dimension of 6 × 6 × 6 mm3 reaches, in dependence of the PBF-LB/M parameter set, 99.8%."

card: Paper card. Question: How can the room temperature ductility of an initially brittle refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) with a continuous ordered B2 matrix be improved while maintaining high yield strength?. System: Al0.5NbTa0.8Ti1.5V0.2Zr (Refractory High Entropy Alloy). Processing: 1. Vacuum/argon arc melting followed by hot isostatic pressing (HIP) at 1200 °C for 2 hours under 210 MPa argon. 2. Homogenization at 1200 °C for 24 hours followed by slow cooling (10 °C/min) to room temperature (Condition 1). 3. Solutionizing Condition 1 at 1400 °C for 20 min followed by water quenching (Condition 2). 4. Annealing Condition 2 at 600 °C for 120 hrs followed by water quenching (Condition 3).. Test conditions: Room temperature (RT) and 600 °C uniaxial compression testing at a strain rate of 0.001 s−1; Vickers microhardness (4.9 N load, 15 s dwell); Microstructural characterization via SEM, TEM, and Atom Probe Tomography (APT).. Findings: Condition (1) (continuous B2 matrix) exhibited a yield strength of 2035 MPa but only 4.5% compressive strain before fracture.; Condition (2) (single-phase weakly ordered BCC) showed high ductility with no fracture after 60% true strain but lower yield strength (1065 MPa).; Condition (3) (inverted microstructure with discrete B2 precipitates in continuous BCC matrix) achieved a yield strength of 1345 MPa and 16.9% peak strain with fracture at 38% strain.; At 600 °C, Condition (3) showed anomalous strengthening with a yield strength of 1423 MPa (higher than its RT value of 1345 MPa) and 16.2% plasticity.; APT analysis revealed strong elemental partitioning: B2 phase is rich in Al and Zr, while BCC phase is rich in Nb and Ta.; The microstructure of Condition (3) consists of discrete B2 precipitates (~50 nm) within a continuous disordered BCC matrix, contrasting with Condition (1) where B2 is the continuous matrix.; Condition (1) hardness was 562 ± 16 HV, Condition (2) was 405 ± 11 HV, and Condition (3) was 475 ± 12 HV.. Mechanism: The authors argue that the poor ductility in Condition (1) is caused by the continuous ordered B2 matrix, which is inherently brittle. The improved ductility in Condition (3) is attributed to the 'inversion' of the microstructure, where the continuous phase becomes the more ductile disordered BCC matrix, while the hard B2 phase exists as discrete precipitates providing strengthening. The anomalous strengthening at 600 °C in Condition (3) is speculated to result from competing slip systems in the complex B2 phase (e.g., <001>{110} and <111>{112}) leading to sessile kinks or dislocation debris, similar to mechanisms in Ni3Al.. Limitations: The authors state that the details of the strengthening mechanisms are beyond the scope of the study and that the explanation for the anomalous strengthening at 600 °C is highly speculative. They note that applying classical precipitation hardening models requires parameters (lattice misfit, elastic properties, fault energies) that are difficult to quantify in this complex RHEA.. Future work: The authors recommend additional scientific studies to establish the influence of concentrated alloy additions on precipitation strengthening parameters, further investigation of deformation mechanisms at room temperature and 600 °C, and additional studies at higher temperatures and under tensile loading.. card: Paper card. Question: Can a single BCC solid solution of NbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloy be successfully fabricated via selective laser melting (SLM) despite the high melting points of its constituent elements, and what are the resulting microstructural, mechanical, and corrosion properties compared to traditional superalloys?. System: NbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloy (nominal equiatomic composition: Nb 99.9%, Mo 99.9%, Ta 99.9%, W 99.9%). Processing: Selective Laser Melting (SLM) using FORWEDO LM120 equipment with a 500 W fiber laser in an argon atmosphere (<20 ppm oxygen); initial parameters: hatch distance 0.1 mm, layer thickness 0.1 mm, laser power factor 0.8, scanning velocity 250 mm/s, S-cross scanning; followed by a remelting process (3 total passes per layer) to achieve a linear energy density of up to 2.83 J/mm. Test conditions: Microstructure and composition analyzed via SEM (HITACHI SU-8010) and EDS; crystal structure via XRD (Cu target, λ = 1.54 Å); microhardness measured on XY plane; corrosion resistance tested via potentiodynamic polarization in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution (scanning voltage −0.2 V to +0.2 V) and high-voltage scanning (−1.5 to +2 V). Findings: A single BCC solid solution was formed without secondary phases, with an experimental lattice parameter of 3.2034 Å.; Elements with lower melting points and densities (Nb and Mo) showed negative molar ratio deviations of up to 3.5% (Nb: −3.5 at%, Mo: −0.16 at%) compared to the nominal 25%.; The average grain size was 13.4 μm, significantly smaller than the 200 μm observed in as-cast NbMoTaW HEA.; Primary and secondary dendrite arm spacings were 6.59 μm and 1.68 μm, respectively, much finer than the 20–30 μm spacing in as-cast samples.; The average microhardness of the SLM-fabricated sample reached 826 Hv, compared to 446 Hv for arc-melted HEA and 310–437 Hv for superalloys.; The free-corrosion current (Icorr) of the NbMoTaW HEA was 8.716 × 10−11 A, which is two orders of magnitude lower than that of 316 L steel (8.815 × 10−9 A).; Visual corrosion testing showed 316 L steel suffered up to 1 mm corrosion depth, while the NbMoTaW alloy exhibited only crack extension and minor pitting.. Mechanism: The rapid solidification in SLM creates extremely high temperature gradients and cooling rates, limiting growth time and resulting in fine grains and slender dendrites. Composition deviations occur because powders with lower melting points and densities fuse first, spread over larger areas, absorb more energy, and evaporate earlier during the process. The improved hardness is attributed to grain refinement following the Hall–Petch law, while superior corrosion resistance is due to the presence of easily passivating elements (Nb, Mo, Ta) despite minor segregation.. Limitations: The ductility of the NbMoTaW HEA at room temperature remains low, and while composition deviation exists (up to 3.5%), it is noted that further study of mechanical properties is still necessary.. Future work: Further study of mechanical properties is required to fully assess the potential of the SLM-fabricated NbMoTaW HEA.. Quote: "The HEA shows an excellent microstructure, microhardness, and corrosion resistance performance compared with traditional superalloys."

card: Paper card. Question: How does varying tungsten concentration affect the crystal structure, microstructure, and mechanical properties (hardness, strength, ductility) of WxNbMoTa refractory high-entropy alloys fabricated via laser cladding deposition?. System: WxNbMoTa refractory high-entropy alloys with x = 0, 0.16, 0.33, 0.53 (mole fractions). Processing: Laser cladding deposition (LCD) using a coaxial LCD system with 565 W laser power, 8 mm/s scanning speed, 0.08 mm layer thickness, and 600 °C induction heating temperature; powders (45–125 μm) mixed for 4 h and dried at 120 °C for 8 h in Argon (<80 ppm O2). Test conditions: Vickers microhardness (500 g load, 30 s); room temperature compression (25 °C, 0.001 s⁻¹); high-temperature compression (1000 °C, 3.5 min heating, 15 min soak, 0.001 s⁻¹ strain rate, 10⁻³ torr vacuum). Findings: All WxNbMoTa alloys formed a single-phase body-centered cubic (BCC) solid solution regardless of tungsten content.; Grain and dendrite sizes averaged 20 μm and 4 μm, respectively, due to rapid solidification in LCD.; Vickers microhardness increased with tungsten concentration: 459.2 ± 9.7, 476.0 ± 12.9, 485.3 ± 8.7, and 497.6 ± 5.6 Hv for x = 0, 0.16, 0.33, 0.53.; NbMoTa (x = 0) exhibited yield strength of 530 MPa and compressive strain of 8.5% at 1000 °C.; At room temperature, NbMoTa showed yield strength of 874 MPa and compressive strain of 5.8%, while W-containing alloys were brittle with compressive strengths of 840–895 MPa.; Bulk modulus increased with tungsten content: 174, 182, 186, and 192 GPa for x = 0, 0.16, 0.33, 0.53.; Spherical gas porosities in as-fabricated samples were eliminated by using molybdenum powders with higher granule density and good sphericity.. Mechanism: Rapid solidification during laser cladding deposition (melting in 10⁻³–10⁻² s) suppresses constitutional segregation and promotes fine equiaxed grains. Tungsten addition increases lattice distortion and solid solution strengthening, raising hardness and bulk modulus but reducing ductility at room temperature. Porosity formation is attributed to adsorbed Argon gas in low-density molybdenum powder particles, not microstructure features.. Limitations: Spherical gas porosities appeared in samples fabricated with standard molybdenum powders due to low granule density; tungsten addition reduces room-temperature plasticity, making W-containing alloys brittle.. Future work: The present work provides a theoretical basis for LCD manufacturing of aerospace parts of refractory HEAs with large size, complex structure, and variable composition.. Quote: "The size of the grains and dendrites are 20 μm and 4 μm on average, due to the rapid solidification characteristics of the laser cladding deposition."

W3137485425.title: Research on the structure of Al2.1Co0.3Cr0.5FeNi2.1 high-entropy alloy at submicro- and nano-scale levels

card: Paper card. Question: How does varying the mechanical alloying milling time affect the microstructural evolution, phase constitution, contamination levels, and mechanical properties of the Al0.3NbTa0.8Ti1.5V0.2Zr refractory high-entropy alloy prepared by powder metallurgy?. System: Al0.3NbTa0.8Ti1.5V0.2Zr refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA). Processing: Mechanical alloying in a Fritsch Pulverisette 6 planetary ball mill under high-purity argon (99.9999%) using hardened steel balls (AISI 52100, 15 mm diameter) at 250 RPM with a 10:1 ball-to-powder weight ratio; followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 1200 °C, 50 MPa uniaxial pressure, 100 °C·min−1 heating rate, and 15 min dwell time.. Test conditions: Milling times of 0, 1, 3, 5, 10, 20, 30, 40, and 50 h; sintering of powders milled for 3, 10, 30, and 50 h; microstructural analysis via XRD, SEM, EDS, and EBSD; mechanical testing via Vickers microhardness (0.2 kgf, 10 s), nanoindentation (100 mN max load), and ultrasound methods.. Findings: After 10 h of milling, the powder achieves 95 wt.% BCC phase with virtually full homogeneity and no significant segregation.; Carbide formation (ZrC) is detected in sintered bulks as early as after 3 h of powder milling.; Oxides (TiO2) are observed in bulks prepared from powders milled for 30 h and 50 h.; The bulk produced from 50 h milled powders exhibits the highest hardness of 675.7 ± 9.8 HV0.2.; The bulk produced from 3 h milled powders exhibits the lowest hardness of 592.9 ± 21.0 HV0.2.; The average grain size of the BCC matrix decreases from 33.8 µm (3 h milling) to 25.2 µm (50 h milling).; Iron contamination increases from undetectable levels to 1.8 at.% (30 h) and 2.2 at.% (50 h) due to milling media wear.; The elastic modulus increases slightly from 134.7 GPa to 138.7 GPa as milling time increases.. Mechanism: Longer milling times induce severe plastic deformation, reducing powder particle size and creating more refined microstructures in the sintered bulks; this refinement, combined with the Hall–Petch effect and the dispersion strengthening from carbides and oxides formed due to contamination from the steel milling media and graphite dies, leads to increased hardness and elastic modulus.. Limitations: The method is highly susceptible to contamination, leading to the formation of oxides and carbides even when using controlled atmospheres; prolonged milling increases contamination levels (C, O, Fe) which may negatively impact ductility.. Future work: The authors suggest exploiting the formation of oxides/carbides as a way of exploring the oxide dispersed strengthening (ODS) effect, which may play an important role in the strengthening mechanisms of HEAs.. Quote: "Ten hours of milling seems sufficient for achieving an optimal equilibrium between microstructural homogeneity and refinement, high hardness and minimal contamination."

card: Paper card. Question: Can a reduced-activation WxTaTiVCr high-entropy alloy and its W-rich derivatives be fabricated via elemental powder mixing and spark plasma sintering to achieve enhanced hardness and strength for fusion plasma-facing applications?. System: WxTaTiVCr high-entropy alloys with W content ranging from 32 to 90 at.% (nominal 30-90 at.%), containing in-situ TiC; specific samples denoted as 32 Ws to 90 Ws.. Processing: Elemental powders (W, Ta, Ti, V, Cr) mixed via Turbula shaker (30 rpm, 3 hours); consolidated via spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 1600 °C, 50 MPa axial pressure, 100 °C/min heating rate, 10 minutes dwell time, under vacuum (10⁻³ torr) in graphite molds.. Test conditions: Micro-Vickers hardness test (1 kg load, 10 s dwell); room-temperature compression test (strain rate 10⁻³/s); XRD, SEM-EDS, TEM, EPMA, and ICP-OES characterization.. Findings: Hardness increased to ~790 Hv for the 42 Ws sample, which is more than twofold higher than pure tungsten (~350 Hv).; Compressive yield strength increased to ~2200 MPa for the 32 Ws sample, approximately twice that of pure tungsten.; In-situ TiC formation was confirmed with a volume fraction varying from 1.1% to 8.5% and irregular sizes between 10 to 25 µm.; C15 cubic Laves phases formed in V- and Cr-rich regions in samples with W content exceeding 70 at.% (71 Ws, 77 Ws, 90 Ws).; Relative density increased as W content decreased, with the 32 Ws sample showing the highest density due to liquid-phase assisted sintering.; Grain sizes were ~30–50 µm for samples with 32–63 at.% W (liquid-phase sintering) and ~3 µm for samples with 71–90 at.% W (solid-state sintering).; The BCC crystal structure was confirmed for the HEA matrix with a lattice parameter of 0.317 nm, while TiC exhibited an FCC structure with a lattice parameter of 0.43 nm.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the enhanced hardness and strength primarily to solid-solution strengthening caused by differences in atomic radii of the constituents, which hinders dislocation movement, and dispersion strengthening provided by the in-situ TiC particles. Additionally, grain boundary strengthening from TiC and the Hall-Petch effect from smaller grain sizes in high-W alloys contribute to the mechanical properties.. Limitations: The study notes that while the chemical composition meets reduced-activation criteria, the actual reduced-activation behavior, irradiation resistance, hydrogen retention, and high-temperature mechanical properties have not yet been analyzed and require future investigation.. Future work: The authors propose that analysis of reduced-activation behavior, irradiation resistance, hydrogen retention, and high-temperature mechanical properties is necessary prior to utilizing the material as an armor material in future fusion reactors like DEMO.. Quote: "A mechanical examination of the samples revealed a more than twofold improvement in the hardness and strength due to solid-solution strengthening and dispersion strengthening."

card: Paper card. Question: How does varying the Ti concentration (X = 0.3, 0.5, 0.7) in Ni1.5Co1.5CrFeTiX high entropy alloys affect their tensile properties, phase composition, and microstructure when processed via powder metallurgy?. System: Ni1.5Co1.5CrFeTiX alloys with X = 0.3, 0.5, and 0.7 (target atomic %: Ni28Co28Cr19Fe19Ti6, Ni27Co27Cr18Fe18Ti9, Ni26Co26Cr17Fe17Ti12). Processing: Mechanical alloying (dry milling for 35 h at 250 rpm, wet milling for 1 h in ethanol) followed by spark plasma sintering (1150 °C, 30 MPa, 10 min dwell) and annealing at 1100 °C for 24 h with water cooling. Test conditions: Room temperature tensile testing at a cross-head speed of 0.25 mm/min; microhardness testing with 100 g load (HV0.1). Findings: Annealed Ti0.7A alloy achieved an ultimate tensile strength of ~1680 MPa with a ductility of ~9%.; Annealed Ti0.5A alloy exhibited an ultimate tensile strength of ~1200 MPa and a ductility of ~14%.; Annealed Ti0.3A alloy showed the lowest strength (845 MPa UTS) and ductility (~2%) due to porosity-induced premature fracture.; Average porosity in Ti0.3A decreased from 3.77% after sintering to 0.43% after annealing.; Lattice parameter increased from 3.58 Å in Ti0.3A to 3.60 Å in Ti0.7A, correlating with increased Ti concentration.; Average oxide particle size increased from below 100 nm in sintered alloys to 150–175 nm in annealed alloys.; The highest strain hardening (Rm–Rp0.2) was observed in the strongest material, Ti0.7A.. Mechanism: Ti increases strength by increasing the average atomic size misfit, thereby enhancing solid solution strengthening; however, high Ti concentrations also drive the formation of intermetallic phases (L12 or DO24) which are suppressed by the rapid cooling of the SPS process.. Limitations: The study notes that the oxide contamination was significantly larger due to the use of ethanol wet-milling, and the precise chemical character of the oxides could not be measured precisely due to EDS resolution limits and signal contamination from the matrix.. Future work: The authors suggest that the oxides could be modified by adding elements with higher oxygen affinity (e.g., Y, Ce) to form more favorable and finer oxide dispersions, and that these alloys may serve as guidelines for designing inclusion-tolerant materials for sustainable metallurgy.. Quote: "Ti increases the strength of the alloys by increasing the average atomic size misfit i.e., solid solution strengthening."

card: Paper card. Question: How can a comprehensive, updated database of mechanical properties and observed phases for multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs) be compiled to aid in identifying design space gaps and training machine learning models?. System: 630 multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs), including complex concentrated alloys (CCAs) with 3 or more principal elements, covering single-phase BCC, single-phase FCC, and multiphase/other microstructures.. Processing: Data extraction from 265 articles (including 136 new articles published in 2019) using keyword search for 'high entropy alloy' on Web of Science; data digitized from plots using webplotdigitizer and combined with previous reviews from 2018.. Test conditions: Mechanical testing performed under tension (T) or compression (C) at various temperatures; properties extracted include yield strength, ultimate tensile/compression strength, elongation, hardness, and Young's modulus.. Findings: The database contains 1545 records from 265 articles, representing a > 100% improvement in available data compared to 2018 reviews.; The study extracted 334 unique MPEA compositions (931 composition-property combinations) in addition to the 296 unique compositions from previous reviews.; Data fields include normalized alloy composition, experimentally observed phases, processing method, grain size, density, and interstitial contents (O, N, C).; Extreme values in property distributions were identified using box plots and investigated for removal or correction.; The database is hosted on Citrination and includes Physical Information File (PIF) records for machine learning applications.; Visualizations of yield strength vs. elongation and temperature dependence of yield strength were generated to guide future research.. Mechanism: The authors explain that the large compositional design space of MPEAs (e.g., 143,000 potential 5-component systems) makes experimental examination of each system prohibitively expensive, necessitating data-driven methods and accurate data accounting to accelerate exploration.. Limitations: Not all properties in the database are reported for every record; specifically, grain size and interstitial contents are missing from many articles despite their importance for refractory MPEAs.. Future work: Researchers are encouraged to contribute new data to the database via a template on GitHub and upload to Citrination to ensure routine updating and improved predictive capabilities for machine learning models.. Quote: "The database contains 1545 records from 265 articles."

card: Paper card. Question: How do the synthesis methods and operating temperatures influence the microstructure, mechanical properties, and tribological performance (friction and wear) of high-entropy coatings (HECs) in various industrial applications?. System: High-entropy coatings (HECs) including metallic (e.g., CuMoTaWV, FeCoCrNiMo0.2, AlCrTiV), ceramic (e.g., (AlCrNbSiTiMo)N, TiVCrZrWNx), and composite systems; base elements include Cr, Fe, Co, Ni, Al, Ti, V, Mo, W, Ta, Nb, Zr, Si, Cu, Mn.. Processing: Fabrication via vapor deposition (magnetron sputtering, reactive sputtering, vacuum arc), thermal spraying (atmospheric plasma spray (APS), high velocity oxy-fuel (HVOF)), and cladding (laser, plasma). Key parameters include substrate bias voltage (0 to -200 V), nitrogen flow rate (FN), substrate temperature (300 °C), annealing (300 °C), and feedstock preparation (mechanical alloying, gas atomization).. Test conditions: Tribological testing performed using ball-on-disk and pin-on-disk setups against counterfaces of Si3N4, Al2O3, and steels (SKH51, 100Cr6, GCR15). Tests conducted from room temperature (RT) up to 600 °C, varying sliding speeds, loads, and sliding distances.. Findings: The CuMoTaWV coating exhibited adaptive tribological behavior: lowest coefficient of friction (COF) and wear rate at RT due to Ta- and W-rich tribo-layers; galling wear at 200 °C; reduced wear at 400 °C due to adaptive CuO formation; and low COF but slightly higher wear at 600 °C due to excessive V-rich phase oxidation.; In (AlCrNbSiTiMo)N coatings, increasing substrate bias from 0 V to -200 V increased hardness from 28.2 GPa to 34.5 GPa and reduced wear rate to 1.2 × 10−6 mm3/N.m at -100 V, attributed to grain boundary strengthening and denser structure.; The (AlCrTiVZr)N film deposited at a nitrogen flow of 12 sccm achieved super-hardness of 41.8 GPa and a low wear rate of 2.3 × 10−7 mm3/N.m.; The FeCoCrNiMo0.2 coating fabricated via APS showed a volume wear rate of 3.9 × 10−5 mm3/N.m, significantly lower than the HVOF coating (4.8 × 10−4 mm3/N.m) and the substrate (5.4 × 10−4 mm3/N.m).; TiVCrZrWNx coatings formed a self-lubricating V2O5 phase during rolling friction, reducing the friction coefficient to 0.38.; The (CrNbSiTiZr)C film exhibited a minimum friction coefficient of 0.3 and a wear rate of 4.2 × 10−6 mm3/N.m due to the formation of a transfer film and high H/E (0.151) and H3/E2 (0.747) ratios.; Annealing the CuMoTaWV film at 300 °C improved its adhesion and wear resistance at both room temperature and 300 °C compared to the as-deposited state.. Mechanism: Tribological improvements are attributed to the formation of self-lubricating oxide layers (e.g., CuO, MoO3, V2O5) at elevated temperatures, the high hardness and nano-crystalline grain structure of the coatings, the presence of secondary phases (e.g., V-rich zones), and the balance between hardness and toughness enhanced by substrate bias or plasma nitriding. Wear mechanisms vary from adhesive wear and galling at intermediate temperatures to mild abrasive wear and oxidative wear at higher temperatures.. Limitations: The text notes that results from different wear experiments using different tools and parameters may not be directly comparable. It also highlights that there is very limited information available regarding high-entropy coatings developed by vapor deposition and cold spray methods compared to thermal spraying and cladding.. Future work: The authors state that further investigation is needed to optimize process parameters, explore more manufacturing processes (especially for HEA wires and targets), and conduct more extensive and interdisciplinary tribological investigations at high temperatures to better understand the complex wear-related phenomena.. Quote: "At RT, the lowest COF and wear rate was observed due to the formation of the Ta- and W-rich tribo layer in the wear track."

Paper card. Question: How does the addition of Silver (Ag) and the variation in temperature affect the tribological properties and wear mechanisms of plasma-sprayed Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti-based high-entropy coatings?. System: Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti-Ag (HEA-Ag) and Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti (HEC) coatings formed on carbon steel. Processing: Plasma spraying. Test conditions: Temperature range from 25 to 750 °C; ball-on-disk sliding; counterface not explicitly named in the specific Li et al. summary but implied standard tribological testing. Findings: At high temperatures (600–750 °C), the HEA-Ag coating achieved a friction coefficient of 0.253 and a wear rate of 0.89 × 10−5 mm3/N.m at 750 °C.; The wear rate of both HEA and HEA + Ag coatings was significantly lower than that of tool steels SKH 51 and Q 125 at all test temperatures.; At low temperatures (RT to 400 °C), tribological properties depended on mechanical properties and Ag lubrication.; The addition of Ag had little effect on the friction coefficient at high temperatures.; The as-sprayed coatings comprised a major FCC solid solution with minor BCC phase.; A lubricious film consisting of Ag and various oxides formed on the frictional surface.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the outstanding tribological properties at high temperatures to the formation of a lubricious film on the frictional surface consisting of Ag and various oxides, which contributes to low friction and wear. At low temperatures, the properties are governed by the mechanical properties of the coating and the solid lubrication provided by Ag.. Limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations for this specific study, only that the study investigated the effect of Ag addition and temperature.. Quote: "a relatively low friction coefficient (0.253) and wear rate (0.89 × 10−5 mm3/N.m) was achieved at 750 °C for HEA-Ag coating"

card: Paper card. Question: How can High-Entropy Alloys (HEAs) be designed and optimized to simultaneously achieve high saturation magnetization, high electrical resistivity, and high malleability for soft magnetic material applications?. System: FeCoNi(AlSi)x where x ranges from 0 to 0.8 in molar ratio (alloys denoted A0 to A8). Processing: Arc-melting pure elements (>99.5 wt.% purity) in high-purity argon atmosphere on a water-cooled Cu hearth, remelted four times for homogeneity; rapid solidification into ingots; compressive testing of cylindrical samples (Φ3 × 6 mm) at room temperature with a strain rate of 2 × 10−4 s−1. Test conditions: Room temperature compressive testing; X-ray diffraction (30 kV, 20 mA, Cu target, 10°/min); Electrical resistivity measurement; Magnetization curves via Physical Property Measurement System (PPMS); SEM-EDS microstructural analysis. Findings: The optimal balance of properties is achieved at x = 0.2 (A2 alloy) with saturation magnetization of 1.15 T, coercivity of 1,400 A/m, electrical resistivity of 69.5 μΩ·cm, yield strength of 342 MPa, and strain without fracture of 50%.; Saturation magnetization (Ms) drops almost monotonically from 1.315 T at x = 0 (A0) to 0.46 T at x = 0.8 (A8) upon Al and Si addition.; Alloys with x ≤ 0.2 exhibit a single-phase FCC solid solution, while x = 0.3 shows a BCC + FCC mixture, and x ≥ 0.4 transitions to almost entirely BCC structure.; Plastic deformation (εp) exceeds 50% without fracture for x in the range of 0 to 0.2, whereas ductility diminishes significantly for x ≥ 0.4, with A8 shattering immediately after elastic deformation.; Electrical resistivity generally increases from x = 0 to x = 0.8, reaching 69.5 μΩ·cm at x = 0.2, which falls within the typical range (50–80 μΩ·cm) of silicon steels.; The A3 alloy (x = 0.3) exhibits a yield strength of 938 MPa and ultimate tensile strength of 2,857 MPa with 33% plasticity, attributed to the mixture of FCC and BCC phases.; Coercivity (Hc) is low for x ≤ 0.2 but increases dramatically at x = 0.3 due to phase boundaries hindering domain-wall movement, before falling back at x = 0.5.. Mechanism: High saturation magnetization in FCC structures is attributed to higher atomic packing density (more ferromagnetic atoms per unit volume) and the absence of anti-parallel magnetic coupling elements like Cr; electrical resistivity increases due to lattice distortion from Al/Si, chemical randomness acting as point defects, and electron scattering; mechanical strength and malleability are governed by the phase composition (FCC favors plasticity, BCC increases lattice resistance) and solid-solution strengthening from lattice distortion.. Limitations: The text notes that for x ≥ 0.4, ductility diminishes and samples become brittle; the A8 alloy shatters immediately after elastic deformation; coercivity is highly sensitive to microstructure and difficult to predict solely from composition; ab initio calculations systematically overestimate saturation magnetization compared to experiments due to limited system size and ignored impurities/phase segregation.. Future work: The authors suggest that coercivity can be tuned within a wide range at a given composition by controlling quenching rates and applying heat/pressure treatments to further reduce Hc; the insights on composition-dependent structures and properties can guide the design of structural and functional HEAs and the development of high-entropy soft magnetic materials.. Quote: "the optimal balance of magnetic, electrical, and mechanical properties is achieved at x = 0.2, for which the combination of saturation magnetization (1.15 T), coercivity (1,400 A/m), electrical resistivity (69.5 μΩ·cm), yield strength (342 MPa), and strain without fracture (50%) makes the alloy an excellent SMM."

card: Paper card. Question: How do the surface morphology, particle size distribution, and microstructure of AlCoCrFeNiSi high-entropy alloy powders evolve during mechanical alloying, and what are the resulting coating properties when deposited via atmospheric plasma spraying?. System: AlCoCrFeNiSi high-entropy alloy (equimolar mixture of Al, Co, Cr, Fe, Ni, Si elemental powders). Processing: Mechanical alloying in a high-energy planetary ball mill (QM-3SP2) at 300 r·min−1, ball-to-powder weight ratio 10:1, powder loading 90 g for 5, 10, 20, and 30 h; coating deposition via atmospheric plasma spraying (APS) using 10 h milled powder, 45 kW arc power, 100 mm spray distance, 200 mm·s−1 traverse speed, with argon primary gas (0.4 MPa) and nitrogen secondary gas (0.3 MPa). Test conditions: Room temperature microhardness testing (200 g load, 10 s dwell); wear testing using a Si3N4 ball (Φ 5 mm) at 5 N load, 573 r·min−1 rotation speed, 5 mm friction radius, for 30 min; XRD (2θ 20–90°, 3°·min−1); FESEM and TEM characterization. Findings: Particle size first increased then decreased with milling time; at 10 h, a narrow peak range from several micrometers to about 50 μm was obtained.; At 10 h milling, simple body-centered cubic (BCC) and face-centered cubic (FCC) solid solution phases were formed with an average grain size of 11.7 nm and lattice strain of about 0.73%.; After plasma spraying, the lamellar structure inside a single particle disappeared, and an ordered BCC phase was detected while Si diffraction peaks vanished.; Transmission electron microscopy revealed nanometer crystalline grains with a grain size of about 30 nm in the APS coating.; The coating exhibited an average microhardness of 612 ± 41 HV.; The volume wear rate of the coating was (0.38 ± 0.08) × 10−4 mm3·N−1·m−1, approximately half that of a previously studied AlCoCrFeNiTi coating.; Wear mechanisms included adhesive wear, tribo-oxidation wear, and slight abrasion wear.; The coefficient of friction reached a steady state average of 0.57 ± 0.02 after an initial running-in stage of 6 min.. Mechanism: During mechanical alloying, plastic deformation and cold welding dominate initially, increasing particle size, followed by work hardening and fracture which reduce particle size and refine the lamellar structure. During plasma spraying, high temperatures cause melting and elemental rearrangement, leading to the disappearance of the lamellar structure, formation of an ordered BCC phase, and dissolution of Si elemental peaks. The high hardness and formation of hard tribofilms contribute to the coating's good wear resistance.. Limitations: The text notes that unmelted and semi-melted particles were present in the coating due to stochastic heating, and that limited interlamellar bonding ratio (less than one third) in thermally sprayed coatings can deteriorate mechanical properties.. Future work: The authors state the coating is promising for use in abrasive environments in industries such as petroleum, power, and mining, implying future application in these sectors.. Quote: "At the milling time of 10 h, simple body-centered cubic (BCC) and face-centered cubic (FCC) solid solution phases were formed."

W4220727698.title: Microstructural and Tribological Behavior of Thermal Spray CrMnFeCoNi High Entropy Alloy Coatings

card: Paper card. Question: How do crystal structure (FCC, BCC, FCC+BCC), temperature, and alloying elements influence the dry sliding wear rate, hardness, and coefficient of friction of high-entropy alloys?. System: Ingot cast high-entropy alloys including the Cantor alloy (CrMnFeCoNi) and its variations (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi, CoCrFeNiTiAl, CoCrFeNiCu, CoCrFeNiS), categorized by FCC, BCC, and dual-phase (FCC+BCC) crystal structures.. Processing: Manufacturing methods include arc melting (most common), vacuum arc melting, induction melting, and spark plasma sintering (SPS); ingots are remelted multiple times for homogeneity, and composites are prepared by mixing powders (e.g., with MoS2, graphite, Ag) before sintering.. Test conditions: Dry sliding conditions using ball-on-disk, pin-on-disk, and ball-on-block setups; counter bodies include Si3N4, Al2O3, and steels (SKH51, 100Cr6, GCR15); tests conducted at room temperature and elevated temperatures (up to 600°C and beyond); loads and sliding velocities varied (e.g., 5 N, 0.28 m/s).. Findings: HEAs with a BCC structure showed superior hardness and wear properties compared to FCC and FCC+BCC alloys due to reduced ductility and limited slip systems.; The addition of Al and Ti to the Cantor alloy increased hardness by up to 40% and promoted a transition from FCC to harder BCC phases.; Wear rates for most HEAs decreased after reaching a certain elevated temperature due to the formation of a protective oxide layer at the sliding interface.; The addition of 0.2 to 1 at.% Cu to CoCrFeNi HEA reduced the wear rate at 600°C by 40–45% due to the lubricating nature of Cu at high temperatures.; Self-lubricating composites with MoS2 and graphite showed significantly lower coefficients of friction but higher wear rates above 200°C compared to the base SPSed HEA.; FCC phase HEAs exhibited higher coefficients of friction and lower hardness compared to BCC phase HEAs, resulting in larger wear tracks.; The addition of V increased hardness but subsequently increased the wear rate after a certain percentage was added.. Mechanism: The superior wear resistance of BCC phases is attributed to limited slip systems causing strong but brittle behavior. At elevated temperatures, wear reduction is driven by the formation of a protective oxide layer (tribo-oxidation) or self-lubricating phases (e.g., CrxSy, sheared Cu) that reduce friction and protect the surface. The 'cocktail effect' and lattice distortion contribute to solid solution strengthening and high hardness.. Limitations: The review notes that intrinsic brittleness in BCC alloys is a trade-off for wear resistance. The oxidation mechanisms are complex due to multiple elements, and the influence of individual elements can taper off or become ill-advised at certain ratios (e.g., excessive brittleness from C or Cr3C2). Manufacturing homogeneity is challenging due to varying densities and melting points.. Future work: Future studies should focus on understanding tribo-oxidation behavior in different environmental conditions, creating guidelines for selecting solid lubricants, exploring additive manufacturing techniques (e.g., laser powder bed fusion) for HEA composites, and conducting detailed cost-performance matrix studies against conventional alloys.. Quote: "In general, HEAs with a BCC structure showed superior hardness and wear properties compared to FCC and FCC + BCC alloys."

W3046832734.title: Synthesis and Characterization of High Entropy Alloy and Coating

card: Paper card. Question: How can a Pt-based high-entropy alloy be designed and synthesized to achieve superior oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) activity and stability compared to commercial Pt/C catalysts in acidic media?. System: PtFeCoNiCu high-entropy alloy (PFCNC-HEA) nanoparticles with atomic ratio 1.0:2.4:1.9:1.8:2.0 and 2 wt% Pt loading. Processing: Impregnation reduction method: metal precursors (Co(acac)2, Fe(acac)3, Ni(acac)2, Cu(acac)2, H2PtCl6·6H2O) dissolved in water/alcohol, mixed with Vulcan XC-72 carbon support, dried at 70 °C, annealed at 700 °C for 30 min under flowing H2/Ar. Test conditions: Three-electrode system in 0.1 M HClO4 at room temperature; Accelerated durability test (ADT) 0.6–1.1 V vs RHE for 10k cycles; Chronoamperometry at 0.7 V for 40,000 s; PEMFC with 0.03 mgPt cm−2 cathodic loading at 0.5–2.0 bar O2 pressure. Findings: Mass activity of 1.738 A mg−1Pt at 0.90 V, which is 15.8 times higher than commercial Pt/C (0.116 A mg−1Pt); Half-wave potential (E1/2) of 0.88 V, 30 mV higher than Pt/C (0.85 V); Negligible voltage decay of 3 mV after 10,000 ADT cycles, compared to 33 mV for Pt/C; Maintains 90.23% of initial current after 40,000 s chronoamperometry, surpassing Pt/C (55.34%); Maximum power density of 1.380 W cm−2 at 2.0 bar O2 pressure with 0.03 mgPt cm−2 loading; Dissolution energy of Fe becomes positive (1.54 eV) in PFCNC-HEA, inhibiting auto-dissolution compared to pure Fe (−0.465 eV); d-band center of surface Pt atoms downshifts by 0.36 eV relative to pure Pt (111); Activation barriers for O-O bond scission of ∗OOH reduced to 0.291–0.326 eV on PFCNC-HEA vs 0.717 eV on Pt (111). Mechanism: The authors attribute the enhanced performance to the ligand effect causing electron transfer from non-noble metals to Pt, which downshifts the d-band center to optimize oxygen intermediate binding. The high-entropy effect improves thermodynamic stability and inhibits metal dissolution. Additionally, multi-element alloying creates multiple active sites and synergistic interactions that lower the activation barriers for O-O bond scission and facilitate the formation of ∗OOH intermediates.. Limitations: The synthesis method is biased toward low loading catalysts; increasing metal load causes significant particle size growth.. Quote: "It shows remarkable ORR catalytic mass activity of 1.738 A mg−1Pt at 0.90 V, which is 15.8 times higher than that of the state-of-art commercial Pt/C catalyst."

card: Paper card. Question: How can the miscibility gap in bimetallic Co-Mo alloys be overcome to create tunable, highly active catalysts for ammonia decomposition using earth-abundant elements?. System: Quinary CoMoFeNiCu high-entropy alloy nanoparticles (general composition CoxMoyFe10Ni10Cu10 where x + y = 70) and control samples of bimetallic Co-Mo and monometallic Ru. Processing: Carbothermal shock technique involving flash heating and cooling of metal precursors on oxygenated carbon nanofibers; temperature reached 2000–2300 K with ramping rates on the order of 10^5 K s−1 and shock duration of ~55 ms. Test conditions: Ammonia decomposition in a plug flow reactor at 250–600 °C using 5 vol% NH3 (and 100 vol% NH3 for specific tests) at a gas hourly space velocity (GHSV) of 36 L gcat−1 h−1. Findings: HEA-Co25Mo45 achieved a mass-specific reaction rate of 22.1 gNH3 gmetals−1 h−1 at 500 °C, representing an improvement factor of ~19 versus bimetallic Co-Mo and ~3 versus Ru.; The most active catalyst, HEA-Co25Mo45, reached 50% NH3 conversion (T50) at 422 °C, compared to 600 °C for Ru and 600 °C for bimetallic Co-Mo.; The apparent activation energy (Eapp) varied from 64.7 kJ mol−1 for the most active HEA-Co25Mo45 to 123.1 kJ mol−1 for the least active HEA-Co55Mo15.; Nitrogen desorption energy (ΔEN) for HEA-Co25Mo45 was ~79 kJ mol−1, which is very close to the value for Ru (84 kJ mol−1).; Catalytic activity exhibited a volcano-type behavior with respect to nitrogen adsorption energy, peaking at an optimal ΔEN of ~79 kJ mol−1.; The HEA-Co25Mo45 catalyst showed negligible degradation after ~50 hours of continuous operation at 500 °C.; For pure NH3 decomposition, HEA-Co55Mo15 achieved an improvement factor of ~118 versus bimetallic Co-Mo and ~40 versus Ru.; Atomistic modeling confirmed a single solid-solution phase with δ = 5.4% and ΔHmix = 0.65 kJ mol−1, showing no phase segregation up to 1000 K.. Mechanism: The high catalytic activity is attributed to the robust tuning of surface nitrogen binding strength via the Co/Mo ratio; the optimal activity arises from a tradeoff where Co-rich catalysts bind N too weakly (limiting dehydrogenation) and Mo-rich catalysts bind N too strongly (limiting N2 desorption), with the HEA composition allowing access to the optimal intermediate binding energy (~79 kJ mol−1) predicted by the Sabatier principle.. Limitations: The text notes that the peak intensities in XRD patterns are low due to the much smaller particle sizes compared to previously reported HEAs, and that the bimetallic Co-Mo catalysts are constrained by large miscibility gaps in their phase diagram.. Future work: The authors propose designing practical reactors with cascaded catalyst layers having gradually changing nitrogen binding strengths to match the varying concentration of NH3 along the flow, which can be readily achieved by varying the Co/Mo ratios in HEA catalysts.. Quote: "Quinary CoMoFeNiCu nanoparticles are synthesized in a single solid-solution phase with robust control over the Co/Mo atomic ratio, including those ratios considered to be immiscible according to the Co-Mo bimetallic phase diagram."

card: Paper card. Question: How can high-entropy alloy (HEA) nanocatalysts be synthesized to achieve simultaneous high performance for both hydrogen evolution (HER) and methanol oxidation (MOR) reactions, and what is the mechanism behind their enhanced activity and stability?. System: Pt18Ni26Fe15Co14Cu27 high-entropy alloy nanoparticles supported on carbon (Pt18Ni26Fe15Co14Cu27/C). Processing: One-pot oil phase synthesis at 220 °C for 2 hours at atmospheric pressure using metal acetylacetonate precursors, oleylamine, CTAC, glucose, and Mo(CO)6, followed by acetic acid treatment to remove surfactants and dispersion on Ketjen Black-300 carbon.. Test conditions: HER tested in N2-saturated 1 M KOH (LSV scan rate 5 mV s−1, stability via chronoamperometry at 11 mV and 10,000 CV cycles); MOR tested in N2-saturated 1 M KOH + 1 M CH3OH (CV scan rate 20 mV s−1, stability via chronoamperometry at 0.65 V and 1,000 CV cycles).. Findings: The Pt18Ni26Fe15Co14Cu27/C catalyst exhibits an ultrasmall overpotential of 11 mV at a current density of 10 mA cm−2 for HER, compared to 84 mV for commercial Pt/C.; The mass activity for HER is 10.96 A mg−1Pt at −0.07 V vs. RHE, significantly higher than the 0.83 A mg−1Pt of commercial Pt/C.; The catalyst achieves a mass activity of 15.04 A mg−1Pt for MOR, which is 10 times higher than that of Pt/C (1.45 A mg−1Pt).; The catalyst maintains 99% of its current density after 10 hours of chronoamperometry at 11 mV, whereas Pt/C retains only ~53%.; After 10,000 CV cycles, the Pt18Ni26Fe15Co14Cu27/C catalyst shows no obvious negative shift in overpotential, while Pt/C shifts by ~33 mV.; The Tafel slope for HER is 30 mV dec−1 for the HEA catalyst compared to 98 mV dec−1 for Pt/C, indicating faster kinetics.; CO stripping onset potential is 0.391 V vs. RHE for the HEA catalyst, a 181 mV decrease compared to Pt/C (0.572 V), indicating superior CO anti-poisoning.; DFT calculations reveal a low activation barrier of 0.11 eV for water dissociation and a rate-determining step energy barrier of 0.45 eV for MOR.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the performance to a synergistic effect of multi-active sites on the HEA surface, where different elements (Pt, Ni, Fe, Co, Cu) facilitate specific steps: Pt acts as an electron reservoir, Ni and Co dominate the electroactive region near the Fermi level for electron depletion, and Fe stabilizes intermediates. This configuration enables fast site-to-site electron transfer, efficient water dissociation, and optimal binding strength for intermediates, while the lattice distortion and multi-component nature inhibit CO poisoning and structural degradation.. Limitations: The text notes that slight stoichiometry variations (e.g., changing Cu content) lead to slightly lower activity, though the optimal composition is robust; it also mentions that non-noble metals (Ni, Fe, Co, Cu) may leach slightly during electrocatalysis, causing minor stoichiometry variations, although the overall structure remains stable.. Future work: The authors propose that the simple oil phase synthesis strategy and the understanding of the multi-active sites and fast site-to-site electron transfer mechanism will lay the foundation for the preparation of other HEAs and their application in related electrocatalysis.. Quote: "The Pt18Ni26Fe15Co14Cu27/C catalyst exhibits excellent electrocatalytic performance for hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) and methanol oxidation reaction (MOR)."

card: Paper card. Question: How can PtRu-based high-entropy alloys be synthesized with subnanometer dimensions and tailored morphologies to achieve high activity, stability, and CO resistance for alkaline hydrogen oxidation reaction (HOR)?. System: PtRuNiCoFeMo high-entropy alloy subnanometer nanowires (SNWs) with composition Pt/Ru/Ni/Co/Fe/Mo = 29.6/9.3/15.2/15.6/12.2/18.1 (SEM-EDS) or 28.5/6.8/18.6/15.2/10.7/20.2 (ICP-OES). Processing: Synthesis via solvothermal reduction: metal precursors (Pt(acac)2, Ru(acac)3, Ni(acac)2, Co(acac)3, Fe(acac)3, Mo(CO)6), glucose (reducing agent), and STAB (structure-directing agent) dissolved in oleylamine (OAm), heated at 210 °C for 5 h, followed by centrifugation and washing with cyclohexane/ethanol (1:9 v/v). Test conditions: Alkaline HOR in 0.1 M KOH solution purged with H2; accelerated durability test (ADT) for 2000 cycles between -0.1 V and 0.4 V vs. RHE at 500 mV s-1; CO poisoning tests in 0.1 M KOH with 1000 ppm CO/H2; chronoamperometry at 100 mV vs. RHE. Findings: Mass activity of HEA SNWs/C reached 6.75 A mgPt+Ru−1, which is 4.1 times higher than commercial PtRu/C (1.65 A mgPt+Ru−1) and 19.8 times higher than Pt/C (0.34 A mgPt+Ru−1); Specific activity of HEA SNWs/C was 8.96 mA cm−2, 2.4 times higher than PtRu/C (3.77 mA cm−2) and 18.7 times higher than Pt/C (0.48 mA cm−2); Only 6.2% loss in mass activity was observed after 2000 ADT cycles for HEA SNWs/C, compared to 20.6%, 31.5%, and 35.3% losses for HEA NPs/C, PtRu/C, and Pt/C respectively; In the presence of 1000 ppm CO, the limiting current density of HEA SNWs/C decreased by only 5.4% at 100 mV vs. RHE, whereas PtRu/C and Pt/C decreased by 21.3% and 22.7%; Chronoamperometry showed HEA SNWs/C activity decreased by 26.4% after 2000 s in 1000 ppm CO, while PtRu/C decreased by 82.9% and Pt/C completely deactivated after 1130 s; The d-band center of HEA SNWs/C shifted upwards to -3.835 eV compared to -3.732 eV for HEA NPs/C, weakening H* adsorption and facilitating OH* adsorption; DFT calculations revealed the energy barrier for H2O formation on HEA surface was as low as 0.08 eV, much lower than 0.57 eV for Pt and 0.27 eV for PtRu; The binding strength of H* on HEA SNWs/C was weakened to an appropriate level near 0 eV, while OH* binding on Ru was moderate at nearly -0.6 eV. Mechanism: Strong electronic interactions between different metal sites in HEA SNWs regulate the binding strength of protons and hydroxyls; Co and Ni sites maintain stable valence states due to pinning effects by Fe and Mo, while Pt and Ru sites modulate overall electroactivity; the upshifted d-band center weakens H* adsorption and facilitates OH* adsorption, and the low energy barrier for H2O formation (0.08 eV) enables rapid desorption and superior HOR activity. Limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study, though it notes that controlled synthesis of PtRu-based HEAs with tailored morphologies remains a general challenge in the field. Future work: The authors propose that the work provides a viable synthetic route for fabricating Pt-based HEA subnano/nano materials and promotes fundamental research on catalysis and beyond. Quote: "The mass and specific activities of HEA SNWs/C reach 6.75 A mgPt+Ru−1 and 8.96 mA cm−2, respectively"

card: Paper card. Question: How does modifying grain boundary morphology from straight to serrated affect the hot ductility drop, tensile fracture strain, and creep rupture life of a selective laser melting (SLM) fabricated precipitation-strengthened high-entropy alloy at elevated temperatures?. System: Al8Co35Cr18Ni34Ti3Nb2Zr0.005B0.01 (at.%) high-entropy alloy (SLMHEA) with fcc γ matrix and L12 γ′ precipitates. Processing: Selective laser melting (SLM) with 270 W laser power, 1000 mm/s scanning speed, 75 μm hatch distance, and 200°C pre-heat; followed by solution heat treatment at 1120°C for 1 h; HT-1 involved air-cooling to room temperature then aging at 750°C for 48 h; HT-2 involved slow cooling at 1°C/min to 1000°C then air-cooling to room temperature followed by aging at 750°C for 48 h. Test conditions: Tensile tests at 25°C and 650°C with strain rate 10−3 s−1; creep tests at 650°C/650 MPa; molecular dynamic simulations at 650°C under 650 MPa load. Findings: Serrated grain boundary increased tensile fracture strain at 650°C by a factor of 3.5 (from 1.8% to 6.3%); Serrated grain boundary increased creep rupture life at 650°C/650 MPa by a factor of 400 (from 0.58 h to 274 h); Minimum creep strain rate decreased by 96% in the serrated sample (from 6.4 × 10−6 s−1 to 2.4 × 10−7 s−1); Average strain at triple junctions reduced from 28% in straight grain boundaries to 11% in serrated grain boundaries (reduction >50%); HT-2 sample (serrated) exhibited 0.45% creep fracture strain compared to 0.03% for HT-1 (straight); Grain boundary serration wavelength was 3.29 ± 0.38 μm and amplitude was 1.69 ± 0.24 μm in HT-2 samples; Coarse γ′ precipitates in HT-2 had an average size of 1.8 μm, compared to 60.1 nm in HT-1; Geometric factor ϕ for creep rate calculation was 0.017 for serrated boundaries versus 1 for straight boundaries. Mechanism: The slow cooling process coarsens L12 γ′ precipitates which interact with mobile grain boundaries via the Zener drag effect, pinning them and causing undulation (serration). This serrated morphology distributes strains more evenly, reduces local strain concentration at triple junctions by over 50%, acts as a crack deflector to retard intergranular crack propagation, and provides resistance against shear parallel to the grain boundary surface.. Limitations: The thermodynamic database predictions for σ phase, C14 Laves phase, B2 phase, and borides did not match experimental observations, likely due to database inaccuracies or non-equilibrium conditions; the study focuses on a single alloy composition and specific heat treatment parameters.. Future work: The study suggests providing a guideline to develop future high-entropy alloys and design post heat treatments for elevated temperature applications, though specific future experiments are not detailed beyond this general recommendation.. Quote: "serrated grain boundary could render a significant increase in tensile fracture strain and creep rupture life by a factor of 3.5 and 400, respectively."

Question: What is the fundamental mechanism responsible for the loss of ductility with increasing temperature in single-phase face-centered cubic high-entropy alloys, specifically CrMnFeCoNi?. System: Equiatomic Cr20MnFe20Co20Ni20 (single-phase) and nonequiatomic Cr26Mn20Fe20Co20Ni14 (dual-phase with Cr-rich σ). Processing: Arc melting under argon atmosphere, homogenization at 1200°C for 48 hours, hot rolling at 1100°C to 8 mm, cold rolling to 2.4 mm (70% reduction), annealing at 1000°C for 1 hour (single-phase) or 900°C for 1 hour (dual-phase). Test conditions: Quasi-static tensile tests at 25° to 800°C, strain rate 10⁻³ s⁻¹, samples held at temperature for ~10 min before testing. Findings: Ductility loss in single-phase Cr20MnFe20Co20Ni20 occurs at intermediate temperatures (400° to 700°C) with fracture shortly after ultimate tensile stress.; Fracture mode changes from fully ductile transgranular failure at 25°C to mixed brittle intergranular and ductile transgranular failure at 700°C.; Atom probe tomography reveals nanosized regions (~5 nm thickness) at grain boundaries enriched with Cr, Ni, and Mn after testing at 700°C.; No second-phase precipitates were detected along grain boundaries by XRD, TEM, or SEM-EDS after testing at 700°C.; Cr and Ni segregate separately at grain boundaries, while Ni and Mn tend to cosegregate.; The dual-phase Cr26Mn20Fe20Co20Ni14 alloy exhibits increased ductility with temperature and no intergranular embrittlement at 600° and 700°C.; Trace elements C and B segregate at grain boundaries but at concentrations (0.2 at% C, 0.008 at% B) insufficient to form carbides or borides.. Mechanism: Ductility loss is caused by the fast segregation of principal elements (Cr, Ni, Mn) into grain boundaries during deformation at intermediate temperatures, forming nanoclusters that reduce grain boundary cohesion and promote crack initiation. The authors propose that Cr and Ni segregate separately due to repulsion, while Ni and Mn cosegregate, potentially forming brittle phases or reducing cohesion via magnetic contributions. Preexisting Cr-rich σ phases can absorb these embrittling elements, preventing their segregation to grain boundaries.. Limitations: The study notes that grain refinement in HEAs can assist the segregation of principal elements to grain boundaries and lead to brittle intermetallic phases, making grain refinement ineffective for avoiding this specific embrittlement. Additionally, the dual-phase alloy designed for proof-of-concept has lower ductility than the single-phase alloy below 500°C.. Future work: The authors suggest that the ductility of HEAs at intermediate temperatures can be further improved if the morphology, dimension, and distribution of secondary phases are optimized further following the proposed GB segregation engineering strategy.. Quote: "Nanoclustering Cr, Ni, and Mn separately at GBs, as detected by atom probe tomography, reduces GB cohesion and promotes crack initiation along GBs."

card: Paper card. Question: How can a hierarchical microstructure be induced in a single crystal high entropy superalloy (HESA) to achieve superior high-temperature tensile yield strength and ductility compared to advanced single crystal superalloys?. System: Ni48.3Co16.9Al10.2Fe8.9Cr7.4Ti5.8Nb1.2Mo0.9W0.4 (at.%) single crystal high entropy superalloy (HESA). Processing: Bridgman casting of single crystal bars; HT-1: single ramp from room temperature to 1,500 K in 20 h followed by air cooling; HT-2: HT-1 followed by additional heat treatment at 1,023 K for 20 h followed by water quenching. Test conditions: Tensile tests conducted at 298 K, 723 K, 923 K, 1,023 K, and 1,173 K with a constant strain rate of 10⁻³ s⁻¹. Findings: HESA in HT-2 state achieved a tensile yield strength of 1,023 MPa at 1,023 K, which is 110 MPa higher than CMSX-4.; The cost-specific yield strength of HESA is 8 times that of CMSX-4.; HESA exhibited a tensile elongation greater than 20% at 1,023 K, which is three times greater than that of CMSX-4.; The HT-2 microstructure contains a dispersion of nano-sized disordered FCC particles (4 nm radius, 4.3 vol%) inside ordered L12 precipitates.; The presence of nano HE-FCC particles contributed an estimated 110 MPa increase in yield strength compared to the HT-1 state.; The average L12 precipitate size increased from 143 nm in HT-1 to 153 nm in HT-2.; At 1,173 K, the HE-FCC particles disappeared, and the yield strength of HT-1 and HT-2 states became similar.; The raw material cost of HESA is 84% cheaper than CMSX-4 due to the absence of Re element content.. Mechanism: The formation of nano-sized disordered FCC particles inside the ordered L12 precipitates is driven by the supersaturation of FCC phase formers within the L12 phase during the HT-1 cooling process; these particles act as obstacles that pin superdislocations, increasing the energy required for dislocation motion and thereby enhancing yield strength.. Limitations: The metastable FCC particles inside the L12 phase are thermodynamically unstable and tend to dissolve into the surrounding FCC matrix after prolonged ageing (e.g., 200 h at 1,023 K) or at higher temperatures (1,173 K), leading to a loss of the hierarchical strengthening effect.. Future work: Future alloy design should utilize slow-diffusing species such as Mo to prolong the dissolution rate of FCC particles and improve the thermal stability of the hierarchical microstructure for creep resistance.. Quote: "A hierarchical microstructure strengthened high entropy superalloy (HESA) with superior cost specific yield strength from room temperature up to 1,023 K is presented."

card: Paper card. Question: How does the addition of Molybdenum (Mo) affect the high-temperature mechanical properties and corrosion resistance of non-equal molar Co-free AlCrFeMnNi BCC high-entropy alloys?. System: Al0.4CrFe1.5MnNi0.5Mox (x = 0 and 0.1). Processing: Vacuum arc melting of elements with >99.9 wt% purity, ingots re-melted at least three times, forged at 1200 °C with 50% thickness reduction, homogenized at 1200 °C for 6 h followed by air cooling.. Test conditions: Tensile testing at 600 °C with an engineering strain rate of 10−3 s−1; Potentiodynamic polarization and EIS in 0.5 M H2SO4 solution at 25 °C under deaerated conditions.. Findings: Vickers hardness of as-homogenized alloys is between HV 350 and HV 400.; Al0.4CrFe1.5MnNi0.5Mo0.1 exhibited a yield strength of 413 MPa and ultimate tensile strength of 430 MPa at 600 °C.; Corrosion current density (Icorr) decreased from 3200 μA/cm2 to 61 μA/cm2 with the addition of 0.1 mol Mo.; Corrosion potential (Ecorr) shifted from −340 mV to −60 mV upon Mo addition.; Grain size decreased from 410 ± 101 μm to 284 ± 114 μm with Mo addition.; Nano-scale NiAl precipitates (B2-type) with sizes of 26 nm to 43 nm were observed in both alloys.; The σ phase formed along grain boundaries in the Mo-containing alloy, identified by higher Cr and Mo content.; The impedance of the passive layer (Rpass) for the Mo-containing alloy was significantly higher than the base alloy and 304 stainless steel.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the enhanced mechanical strength to slip frustration hardening (SFH) from nano NiAl precipitates and precipitation hardening from the σ phase. For corrosion, the improvement is explained by the formation of a stable MoO3 protective oxide layer in the passive film, which acts as a barrier to electrochemical attack and reduces the dissolution rate of active zones.. Limitations: The text notes that the σ phase precipitation along grain boundaries leads to intergranular fracture, indicating a trade-off where the Mo-containing alloy exhibits a slightly ductile but more brittle fracture mode compared to the base alloy. Additionally, the authors state that further experiments are required to confirm the specific formation of slip systems and dislocation movement.. Future work: Further experiments are required to confirm the formation of the slip system and dislocation movement in Al0.4CrFe1.5MnNi0.5Mox (x = 0 and 0.1) alloys.. Quote: "Al0.4CrFe1.5MnNi0.5Mo0.1 exhibited outstanding tensile properties, with a yield strength of 413 MPa and ultimate tensile strength of 430 MPa in the elevated tensile test at 600 °C"

card: Paper card. Question: What are the individual effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on the microstructure and mechanical properties (yield strength, ductility, and elevated-temperature performance) of equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr refractory high-entropy alloys?. System: Equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr and its five sub-alloys created by the subtraction method: HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi. Processing: Vacuum-arc melting of 99.9 wt.% (99.99 wt.% for Ti) pure elements stacked by melting point, re-melted at least four times, and solidified in a water-cool copper mold. Test conditions: Compression tests at room temperature, 800 °C, 1000 °C, 1200 °C, and 1400 °C; crosshead speed 0.36 mm/min (strain rate 10⁻³ s⁻¹); cylindrical samples 3.6 mm diameter x 6 mm height. Findings: HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy yield strength was 1512 MPa at room temperature and 556 MPa at 1200 °C.; HfMoTaTiZr (Nb removed) showed the highest room temperature yield strength of 1600 MPa but lower toughness.; HfMoNbTaTi (Zr removed) exhibited the best comprehensive properties with 27% fracture strain at room temperature and 367 MPa yield strength at 1400 °C.; The presence of Mo increased room temperature yield strength from 929 MPa (in HfNbTaTiZr) to 1512 MPa but reduced fracture strain from >50% to 12%.; Nb addition increased yield strength by 38% at 1200 °C and significantly improved room temperature fracture strain.; Zr addition increased strength but strongly deteriorated room temperature toughness, reducing fracture strain from 27% to 12%.; Alloys with Mo present showed much better strength at elevated temperatures compared to HfNbTaTiZr.; At 1200 °C, HfMoNbTaTi alloy had the highest specific strength among the tested alloys.. Mechanism: The high yield strength is attributed to the solid solution strengthening effect driven by atomic size and shear modulus mismatch; the high entropy effect promotes the formation of a single BCC disordered solid solution phase despite binary phase diagrams suggesting intermetallics; severe lattice distortion reduces the effective shear modulus by approximately 30% compared to the rule of mixtures.. Limitations: There is a deviation of about 30% between calculated and experimental yield strengths, likely due to overestimated shear modulus; the criteria for Laves phase formation were not fully consistent with experimental observations; the reduction in shear modulus due to lattice distortion requires further research to confirm reasons.. Future work: Further modification of composition and/or anti-oxidation coatings are required for high-temperature applications in air; more research is needed to confirm the elemental effects in other RHEA systems and to understand the reasons for reduced shear modulus.. Quote: "The subtraction method was applied on equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys to discover the role of each element"
